description: What components are, how JSX works, and how props carry data into your UI.

screens.body:
A React app is a tree of components — small, reusable building blocks. A button, a profile card, a whole page: each one is a component.

Under the hood, a component is just a JavaScript function that returns what should appear on screen. Learn that sentence and you've learned the core idea of React.

options: A JavaScript function that returns UI
check.question: What is a React component?

screens.heading: Your UI is built from components
screens.keyPoint: A component = a function that returns UI.

screens.body:
JSX lets you write tags like <h1> right inside your JavaScript file. It looks like HTML, but it's really JavaScript wearing an HTML costume.

Because it's JavaScript, you can drop any expression inside curly braces: {name}, {2 + 2}, even {items.map(...)}. React evaluates it and puts the result on screen.

options: It's JavaScript that looks like HTML
check.question: What's true about JSX?

screens.heading: JSX looks like HTML, but it's JavaScript
screens.keyPoint: JSX = HTML-shaped JavaScript; { } runs real JS.

screens.body:
React uses the capital letter to tell your components apart from built-in HTML tags. <Greeting /> is your component; <div> is just a div.

Write function greeting() with a lowercase g and React will treat it like an unknown HTML tag — your component silently won't work.

options: So React knows it's your component, not an HTML tag
check.question: Why must component names start with a capital letter?

screens.heading: Capitalize your component names
screens.keyPoint: Capital letter = component. Lowercase = HTML tag.

screens.body:
Props are how a parent hands data to a child component — like passing arguments to a function. Same component, different props, different output.

You pass them as attributes: <Greeting name='Roli' />. Inside the component, they arrive bundled in one props object.

options: Data a parent passes into a component
check.question: What are props?

screens.heading: Props feed data into components

screens.body:
Inside the component, grab what you need from the props object: props.name, props.age. You'll often see it shortened with destructuring: function Greeting({ name }).

One rule: props are read-only. A component never changes its own props — if the data needs to change, that decision belongs to the parent.

options: No — props are read-only; the parent owns the data
check.question: Can a component change its own props?

screens.heading: Read props with curly braces

screens.body:
A component must return a single element. Two siblings side by side will fail — wrap them in a <div>, or a fragment <>...</> if you don't want an extra div.

Think of it like a function returning one value: the whole UI tree hangs off that one parent.

options: It's an error — wrap them in one parent element
check.question: What happens if a component returns two elements with no wrapper?

screens.heading: Return one parent element

screens.body:
Real apps nest components like LEGO: an App renders a Header, which renders a Nav, which renders Links. Small pieces snap together into big screens.

This is why components pay off — build a Button once, then drop <Button /> everywhere instead of rewriting the same markup.

options: Nesting small components inside bigger ones
check.question: What does 'composing components' mean?

screens.heading: Compose: components inside components
screens.keyPoint: Small components nest into big UIs.
